segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples, and when he had encouraged them and said farewell, he set out to go to Macedonia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After he had gone through those parts and encouraged them with many words, he came to Greece,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where he spent three months. When the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Beroea, by Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, by Gaius from Derbe and Timothy, and by Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These men arrived and waited for us at Troas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and within five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was speaking to them. Because he was going to leave the next day, he kept talking until midnight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window, sinking into a deep sleep as Paul went on speaking still longer. Overcome by sleep, he fell from the third story to the ground below and was picked up dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul went down, threw himself on him, and put his arms around him, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Stop this commotion, for his life is in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked with them a long while, until dawn; and so he left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought the boy away alive and were not a little comforted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We, meanwhile, went ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, where we intended to take Paul on board; for he had arranged it so, intending to go there by land himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Sailing from there, we arrived the next day off Chios; the day after, we crossed over to Samos, and on the day following we came to Miletus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not have to spend time in Asia; he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if he possibly could, on the day of Pentecost.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to him, he said to them:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: serving the Lord with all humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: how I did not hold back from declaring to you anything that would benefit you, or from teaching you in public and from house to house,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: testifying to both Jews and Greeks about turning back to God and faith in our Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, look, bound by the Spirit I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will meet me there,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in city after city, saying that chains and afflictions await me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I do not count my life as worth anything or as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of the grace of God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, look, I know that none of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will see my face again.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore I bear witness to you this very day that I am clean of the blood of all,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Pay close attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God, which he acquired through his own blood.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and from among your own selves men will rise up and speak twisted things, to draw the disciples away after them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore stay alert, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you with tears.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been made holy.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You yourselves know that these hands provided for my own needs and for those who were with me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In everything I showed you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had said this, he knelt down with them all and prayed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all wept a great deal, and they threw their arms around Paul’s neck and kissed him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they were never going to see his face again. Then they escorted him to the ship.

notes.note: The Greek text translated here has a verb meaning “came” or “arrived.” Many manuscripts, followed by most English versions, have a verb differing by a single letter that means “went ahead.” On either reading this group reached Troas before the narrator’s party did.

The narrative shifts here into the first person plural, last used at Philippi (16:10–17). The usual explanation is that the author, or a source he drew on, rejoined Paul’s company at this point. The origin and significance of these “we” passages are debated.

notes.phrase: On the first day of the week
notes.note: The Greek is a Jewish idiom, literally “on day one of the Sabbaths,” meaning the first day of the week. It is uncertain whether Luke is counting days from sunset, in the Jewish way, which would make this Saturday night, or from morning, which would make it Sunday night. This is among the earliest references to believers gathering on that day.

The verb describes noisy tumult and is related to the noun rendered “uproar” in verse 1. It is used elsewhere of the loud wailing of mourners (Mark 5:39), which fits the scene here. Most translations take it as inward alarm, which is also possible.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering, as in the previous chapter, and the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one word.

Most translations have “repentance,” an established term understood to include a change of life. In current English, however, that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct.

The Greek can mean that Paul is constrained by the Holy Spirit or that he feels bound in his own spirit, that is, inwardly compelled. Most modern translations take it of the Holy Spirit, as here; older versions took it of Paul’s spirit. “Bound” anticipates the “chains” of the next verse, a related word in Greek.

Most translations have “ministry” here. The Greek was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests a clerical profession.

The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, including public proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title. Many modern translations already alternate between the two.

The men addressed are the same people called “elders” in verse 17. The Greek word later came into English as “bishop,” but here it describes the elders’ function of watching over the community, not a separate rank.

The Greek can also be read “through the blood of his Own,” that is, of his own Son, and a number of scholars and some translations prefer this because speaking of God’s blood is so unusual. The rendering here follows the more ordinary grammar of the phrase. Some manuscripts read “the assembly of the Lord” in place of “the assembly of God,” which would remove the difficulty; “of God” is generally judged more likely to be original.

The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and means to bring someone into the sphere of what belongs to God. Most translations use “sanctified,” which hides that link and now suggests to many readers a technical doctrine of gradual moral improvement. The meaning itself is not in dispute.

notes.phrase: It is more blessed to give than to receive
notes.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in any of the four Gospels. Paul cites it as something his hearers are expected to know already, which shows that sayings of Jesus circulated apart from the written Gospels.
